Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: 'Avoid Exercise' is not clinically coherent with the rest of the profile. The threat items center on hypervigilance about nighttime intrusion and safety checking in the home, while the memory and appraisal items focus on intrusive assault memories, danger, and physical vulnerability. Exercise avoidance addresses a different symptom domain and lacks plausible linkage to the selected threat, memory, or appraisal content. In contrast, magical thinking and mirror checking fit better with maladaptive attempts to manage threat and distress.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: These two selected items are difficult to reconcile within the same profile. A strong appraisal of permanent bodily damage implies acknowledgment of serious ongoing physical consequences, whereas telling oneself the event did not really happen or was not that bad reflects minimization/denial of the trauma's reality or impact. While some ambivalence can occur clinically, this pair pulls in opposing directions strongly enough to question internal coherence in this profile.

vignette: Akua had always found solace in her pottery studio, surrounded by the familiar scent of clay and the soothing sound of spinning wheels. But since the assault six months ago, everything felt different. The world, once a place of comfort and creativity, now seemed treacherous, as if danger lurked around every corner. She couldn't shake the feeling that she was constantly at risk, and her body reacted accordingly - her heart racing, her senses on high alert. As a result, Akua found herself engaging in all sorts of behaviors to try and feel safe again. She would check the locks on her studio doors multiple times a day, making sure they were secure, and catch glimpses of herself in mirrors, as if to reassure herself that she was still intact. At night, she'd wake up repeatedly to listen for any sounds that might indicate someone was breaking in, her ears straining to pick up the slightest creak or groan. And when she did manage to fall asleep, the memories of that awful day would force their way into her mind, vivid and unbidden - images of the attacker's face, the feeling of his hands on her skin, the sound of her own screams. These memories were so real, so visceral, that Akua felt like she was reliving the event all over again. She'd try to suppress them, to push them away, but they'd only come back stronger, more insistent. And with each recollection, her conviction grew: the world was a dangerous place, and she was just one misstep away from disaster. This fear seeped into every aspect of her life, making it hard for her to relax even in the safety of her own studio. She'd be working on a piece, lost in the flow of creation, when suddenly her body would tense up, as if anticipating an attack. Akua knew that these thoughts and behaviors were taking a toll on her mental health. She felt like she was walking on eggshells all the time, waiting for the other shoe to drop. But try as she might, she couldn't seem to shake off the feeling of being constantly at risk. Her body seemed to have developed a mind of its own, reacting to every little thing as if it were a threat. And with each passing day, Akua felt herself becoming more and more withdrawn, unable to face the world outside her studio. It was this sense of disconnection that finally brought Akua to seek help. She knew she couldn't keep living like this - trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance, unable to find peace even in her own creative pursuits. As she sat in her therapist's office, surrounded by the familiar sights and sounds of her pottery studio, Akua felt a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, she could learn to navigate this treacherous world again, to find a way back to the sense of safety and security that had once been hers. But for now, the memories still lingered, raw and unprocessed. And as Akua left the therapist's office, she couldn't shake the feeling that she was being watched, that unseen eyes were trained on her from across the room. She quickened her pace, glancing over her shoulder, as if expecting to see her attacker waiting for her in the shadows. The world might be a dangerous place, but Akua was determined to face it head-on - with courage, and with clay.
